event: I have to present to senior leadership next week.
rawInterpretation: I am going to embarrass myself in front of everyone.
alternateRealityChecks: Presentations rarely go perfectly for anyone.
Senior leaders attend many presentations and understand that presenters can feel nervous.
Preparation significantly reduces the likelihood of major issues.
A less-than-perfect presentation is not the same as embarrassment.
revisedInterpretation: I may feel nervous, but that does not mean the presentation will go badly.
chosenBehaviour: Prepare thoroughly and practise key messages.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The presentation was well received and generated useful discussion.

event: I forgot part of what I wanted to say during a presentation.
rawInterpretation: Everyone noticed and thinks I am unprepared.
alternateRealityChecks: Audience members often notice less than presenters think.
Most people do not remember every detail of a presentation.
Pausing to gather your thoughts is normal.
One missed point does not define the overall presentation.
revisedInterpretation: The mistake was likely much more noticeable to me than to the audience.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on recovering smoothly rather than dwelling on the mistake.
outcomeOneWeekLater: No one mentioned the forgotten point.

event: Several people looked at their phones during my presentation.
alternateRealityChecks: People check phones for many reasons unrelated to the speaker.
Some attendees may be handling urgent messages or multitasking.
A few distracted people do not represent the entire audience.
You cannot determine engagement from a single behaviour.
revisedInterpretation: I do not have enough evidence to conclude that the audience was bored.
chosenBehaviour: Continue presenting rather than focusing on individual audience members.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Several participants complimented the presentation afterwards.

event: I stumbled over a few words while speaking.
alternateRealityChecks: Most speakers occasionally stumble over words.
Professionalism is determined by more than perfect delivery.
The audience is likely focused on the message rather than small errors.
Minor speaking mistakes are normal.
revisedInterpretation: The stumble was a minor part of a larger presentation.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The audience remembered the message rather than the mistakes.

event: Someone asked a question I could not answer immediately.
rawInterpretation: People now think I am not knowledgeable.
alternateRealityChecks: No speaker knows everything.
Challenging questions are common in discussions.
Following up later is a professional response.
One unknown answer does not define expertise.
revisedInterpretation: Not knowing one answer does not undermine my credibility.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The audience appreciated the detailed follow-up.

event: I felt extremely nervous before my presentation.
rawInterpretation: My nervousness means I will perform badly.
alternateRealityChecks: Many effective speakers feel nervous before presentations.
Feeling nervous does not accurately predict performance.
Anxiety often reflects importance rather than inability.
Performance and emotions are related but not identical.
revisedInterpretation: I can feel nervous and still present effectively.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The session went smoothly despite nervousness.

event: My presentation received less discussion than expected.
alternateRealityChecks: Limited discussion can occur for many reasons.
The audience may have agreed with the content.
Time constraints may have reduced questions.
The amount of discussion is not a direct measure of value.
revisedInterpretation: The lack of discussion does not automatically indicate poor content.

event: A senior stakeholder challenged one of my points.
rawInterpretation: They think I do not know what I am talking about.
alternateRealityChecks: Questions and challenges are common in professional discussions.
Stakeholders often test assumptions and explore trade-offs.
Challenging an idea is not the same as challenging a person.
The discussion may reflect engagement with the topic.
revisedInterpretation: The challenge may have been directed at the idea rather than me.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The discussion improved the final proposal.

event: I watched a recording of my presentation.
rawInterpretation: I sound awkward and should avoid public speaking.
alternateRealityChecks: Most people are uncomfortable hearing recordings of themselves.
Self-criticism often focuses on imperfections.
Public speaking is a skill that improves through practice.
One recording does not define future ability.
revisedInterpretation: I can identify areas for improvement without concluding that I should avoid speaking.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on one improvement area at a time.

event: There was a long silence after I asked the audience a question.
rawInterpretation: Nobody understands or cares about what I am saying.
alternateRealityChecks: Audiences sometimes need time to think.
Silence does not necessarily reflect disinterest.
People may be considering their response.
There are many possible explanations for the pause.
revisedInterpretation: The silence may simply indicate that people were processing the question.
chosenBehaviour: Allow more thinking time before speaking again.

event: I noticed several mistakes while reviewing my presentation slides after the meeting.
alternateRealityChecks: Imperfections can exist within an otherwise effective presentation.
Audience members often focus on core messages.
Mistakes provide learning opportunities.
The presentation should be evaluated as a whole.
revisedInterpretation: There were areas to improve, but that does not invalidate the overall presentation.
chosenBehaviour: Note lessons learned for future presentations.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Feedback was more positive than expected.

event: People asked more questions than usual after my presentation.
rawInterpretation: My presentation must have been confusing.
alternateRealityChecks: Questions often indicate engagement and interest.
Interested audiences usually ask more questions.
The audience may have wanted to explore the topic further.
Questions alone do not prove confusion.
revisedInterpretation: The questions may indicate engagement rather than confusion.
chosenBehaviour: View questions as opportunities for discussion.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Stakeholders requested additional sessions on the topic.

event: I am presenting at a conference for the first time.
rawInterpretation: I am not experienced enough to be here.
alternateRealityChecks: You were selected or invited for a reason.
Many first-time speakers feel similarly.
Experience grows through participation.
Feeling uncertain does not mean you do not belong.
revisedInterpretation: I may be new to this environment, but that does not mean I am unqualified.
chosenBehaviour: Prepare thoroughly and trust my expertise.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The session was successful and well attended.

event: I forgot one slide during my talk.
rawInterpretation: The audience thinks I am disorganised.
alternateRealityChecks: Many audience members may not have known a slide was skipped.
The overall presentation matters more than one omission.
People evaluate presentations holistically.
The mistake does not reveal what others think.
revisedInterpretation: The skipped slide was a minor issue within a larger presentation.
chosenBehaviour: Move on rather than dwelling on the mistake.

event: Several presentations before mine were delivered by highly experienced speakers.
rawInterpretation: My presentation will look amateurish in comparison.
alternateRealityChecks: Different speakers bring different perspectives and strengths.
Audiences often value authenticity and relevance.
Comparisons do not determine the value of your message.
Experience is only one aspect of effective communication.
revisedInterpretation: My presentation can still provide value even if others are more experienced.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on delivering my message clearly.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The audience responded positively to the practical insights shared.
